examples.visual_actual: matches; but the preceding 'Common Data Set 202\x17-202\x18' header on this page shows the same digit corruption as page 1
examples.note: Letters extract mostly correctly here, confirming corruption is concentrated in/around specific glyphs (control chars) rather than uniform scrambling, but digits are hit.

Confirms digit corruption is not isolated to the year in the document title: '7' in '2017' also renders as a control character (\x1a) here. This means ANY digit in this document's text layer is potentially wrong, not just the cover-page year string — table numbers extracted via text layer cannot be trusted either. Note the substitution is a consistent Caesar-like offset (each visual digit's ASCII code minus 29 gives the control-char byte observed: '4'=0x34-29=0x17, '5'=0x35-29=0x18, '7'=0x37-29=0x1a), so it is a systematic CMap remapping, not random corruption — but still unusable without re-deriving the mapping, which get_text() does not do.

text_layer_corruption.conclusion: Corruption affects digits as well as letters, via a consistent -29 byte offset in the broken ToUnicode CMap (verified: 0x17->'4', 0x18->'5', 0x1a->'7'). Confirmed via page 10: '2017' (a data-bearing year, not just the document title) extracts as '201\x1a'. This means routing logic AND any text-based numeric extraction (enrollment counts, percentages, cohort years) on this document are compromised if they rely on page.get_text(). Only image-based reading is reliable, unless the extraction engine is changed to apply the discovered -29 byte-offset correction to every character (untested beyond the 3 sampled digits, and letters appeared mostly correct in some regions — e.g. page 4 body text extracted cleanly — suggesting the corruption may be scoped to a specific font/character range rather than the whole document; do not assume the offset fix is safe to apply blindly across all text).
